d.g: Of or pertaining to yoga.
d.x: Here we see the yogic pattern, "Loss of semen equals loss of soul."

yogic.e: Proto-Indo-European *yewg- Proto-Indo-European *yówg-os Proto-Indo-Iranian *yáwgas Proto-Indo-Aryan *yáwgas Sanskrit योग॑ (yóga)bor. English yoga Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English yogic From yoga + -ic.

d.g: of or relating to yoga

Distant, but within sight; (that thing) just over there.

d.g: yonder.
That one or those over there.
Acronym of yarn over needle.

yon.e: From Middle English yon, from Old English ġeon, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz. Cognate with Dutch geen and German jener.

d.g: At or in a distant but indicated place.
d.x: See who yonder is.

d.g: The vast distance, particularly the sky or trackless forest.
d.x: She set off into the blue yonder.

yonder.e: From Middle English yonder, yondre, ȝondre, ȝendre, from Old English ġeonre (“thither; yonder”, adverb), equivalent to yond (from ġeond, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz) + -er, as in hither, thither. …

d.g: In the early part of growth or life; born not long ago.
d.x: a lamb is a young sheep

d.g: At an early stage of existence or development; having recently come into existence.
d.x: the age of space travel is still young

d.g: advanced in age; (far towards or) at a specified stage of existence or age.
d.x:
And thou, our Mother, twice two centuries young,
Bend with bright shafts of truth thy bow fresh-strung.

d.g: Junior (of two related people with the same name).
d.x: The young Mr. Chester must be in the wrong, and the old Mr. Chester must be in the right.

young.e: Inherited from Middle English yong, yonge, from Old English ġeong, from Proto-West Germanic *jung, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuHn̥ḱós, from *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”). …

d.g: comparative form of young: more young
d.x: Our neighbors' son is younger than our daughter.

d.g: Synonym of junior.
One who is younger than another.
d.x: Youngers did not like olders to be mean and bossy.

d.g: Somewhat young.
d.x: In spite of his youngish appearance, he had much experience.

youngish.e: English young Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -ish English -ish English youngish From young + -ish.

d.g: Young or seeming young.
d.x: a youthful butler

d.g: Characteristic of young people.
d.x: youthful vivacity

d.g: In a youthful manner.
d.x: Nonetheless, it would be wonderful if, in the face of inevitable fate, all people could live youthfully and vitally until the end.

youthfully.e: English youthful Middle English -ly English -ly English youthfully From youthful + -ly.

d.g: A person who engages in antisocial behaviour or drunkenness.
d.x: Yes, it's holiday time again for British yobs – and the rest of us can flee to those parts of Abroad which the louts ignore, or just cringe in shame at home.

yob.e: Backslang for boy. The second sense was likely influenced by hobnob and/or yokel.

d.g: A yob.
d.x: Yeah, but you heard what Blake said. We wouldn't stand a chance against Pike's mob. They're a right bunch of yobbos.

yobbo.e: English yob English -o English yobbo From yob + -o.

d.g: a unit of information equal to 1024 zebibits or 2^80 bits
Strictly, 2⁸⁰ (1024⁸, 1,208,925,819,614,629,174,706,176) bytes or 2¹⁰ (1024) zebibytes, as opposed to a yottabyte.
Alternative form of yobbo (“person engaging in antisocial behaviour or drunkenness”).
A soldier's female Korean lover or hired prostitute.
A Korean person.

yobo.e: Korean 여보 (yeobo)bor. English yobo Borrowed from Korean 여보 (yeobo, “darling, sweetheart”).

d.g: To sing (a song) in such a way that the voice fluctuates rapidly between the normal chest voice and falsetto.
An act of yodelling.
A song incorporating yodelling.

yodel.e: German jodelnbor. English yodel Borrowed from German jodeln.

d.g: present participle and gerund of yodel
The act of one who yodels.
Alternative spelling of yodeler.
The tenth letter of many Semitic alphabets/abjads (Phoenician, Aramaic, Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic and others).
A tool used to read a Torah.

yodh.e: Borrowed from Hebrew יו״ד (yo"d, “name of the tenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *yad- (“hand”). That letter is used also in other Semitic alphabets; it represents the voiced palatal approximant /j/. Doublet of iota, jot, and yod.

d.g: Any of several Hindu or Buddhist disciplines aimed at training the consciousness for a state of perfect spiritual insight and tranquillity; especially a system of exercises practiced to promote control of the body and mind.
d.x: If you're not into yoga / If you have half a brain / […] / Then I'm the love that you've looked for / Write to me and escape

d.g: The tree Elaeocarpus joga.

yoga.e: Proto-Indo-European *yewg- Proto-Indo-European *yówg-os Proto-Indo-Iranian *yáwgas Proto-Indo-Aryan *yáwgas Sanskrit योग॑ (yóga)bor. …

d.g: one of the main traditions of Mahayana Buddhism;  holds that the mind is real but that objects are just ideas or states of consciousness
Dated spelling of yogurt.
Alternative spelling of yogurt.

d.g: A devotee or adherent of yoga.
d.x: Gurdjieff connects this type of breathing with yogi breathing.

d.g: To turn (someone) into a yogi; to lead into practicing yoga.
To persuade someone to give you food or other favors without actually begging.

yogi.e: From Hindi योगी (yogī), from Sanskrit योगिन् (yogin), from the verbal root yuj (class 7 present युनक्ति (yunakti, “to connect”)), from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.

d.g: A milk-based product stiffened by a bacterium-aided curdling process, and sometimes mixed with fruit or other flavoring.
d.x: Moroccan curried crab and streaks of minty, lemony yogurt add luxury to a supersimple zucchini soup ($14).

d.g: Any similar product based on other substances (e.g. soy yogurt).

yogurt.e: Proto-Turkic *yugur- Proto-Turkic *-t Proto-Turkic *yogrut Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yoğurt)bor. English yogurt Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yoğurt). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yogrut.

d.g: A bar or frame by which two oxen or other draught animals are joined at their necks enabling them to pull a cart, plough, etc.; (by extension) a device attached to a single draught animal for the same purpose.
d.x: The Oxe hath therefore ſtretcht his yoake in vaine, / The Ploughman loſt his ſweat, and the greene corne / Hath rotted, ere his youth attainde a bearde: […]

d.g: Any of various linking or supporting objects that resembles a yoke (sense 1.1); a crosspiece, a curved bar, etc.
d.x: Steam Engines. […] The valve rods are coupled by connecting-rods […] and yokes[…], to eccentrics[…].

d.g: A pole carried on the neck and shoulders of a person, used for carrying a pair of buckets, etc., one at each end of the pole; a carrying pole.
Any of various devices with crosspieces used to control an aircraft; specifically, the control column.

yoke.e: From Middle English yok, yoke, ȝok from Old English ġeoc (“yoke”), from Proto-Germanic *juką (“yoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm (“yoke”), from *yewg- (“to join; to tie together, yoke”). Doublet of yuga, jugum, yoga and possibly yogh. …

d.g: A person from or living in the countryside, viewed as being unsophisticated or naive.
d.x: They love the scenery near their summer home, but have no desire to mix with the local yokels.

yokel.e: First use appears c. 1812, possibly from dialectal German Jokel, diminutive of Jakob, cf. Yankee (“little John”) and jacquerie (“a peasant uprising”). Alternatively, from dialectal English yokel, yuckle (“a European green woodpecker”), itself probably a variant of hickwall.

d.g: port city on southeastern Honshu in central Japan
a Penutian language spoken by the Yokuts in the San Joaquin Valley
The yellow, spherical part of an egg that is surrounded by the white albumen, and serves as nutriment for the growing young.

d.g: The grease in a sheep's fleece; lanolin.
To produce yolk.

yolk.e: From Middle English yolke, yelke, ȝolke, ȝelke, from Old English ġeolca, ġeoloca, ġioleca (“the yellow part, yolk”), derived from Old English ġeolu (“yellow”) + -ca (diminutive suffix).

d.g: A time long past.
d.x: This word comes from the days of yore.

yore.e: From Middle English yore, yoare, yare, ȝore, ȝare, ȝeare, from Old English ġeāra (“long ago”), of unclear origin but probably from Proto-Germanic *jērǫ̂ (literally “of years”), the genitive plural of Proto-Germanic *jērą (“year”). More at year.

d.g: to bowl a yorker at a batsman, especially to get a batsman out in this way.
To vomit.

a series of waterfalls in Yosemite National Park in California;  is reduced to a trickle for part of each year

a yobibit.
One septillion (10²⁴, or 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000) bytes or 1,000 zettabytes.
A yobibyte.

yottabyte.e: English yotta- Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydt Proto-Germanic *bītaną Proto-West Germanic *bītan Old English bītan Middle English biten English bite English byte English yottabyte From yotta- + byte.

d.g: The state or qualities of being young or youthful; youth.
d.x: […] he was conscious of a feeling which independently pronounced him her senior in point of Time, and Isabel a child of everlasting youngness.

youngness.e: English young Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English youngness From young + -ness.

d.g: A young person.
d.x: “Besides,” she says, looking possessively at her class of Chinese youngsters, “can you imagine these children going to an ordinary school?”

youngster.e: From young + -ster. Attested from the early 17th century.

d.g: a city in northeast Ohio
junker

younker.e: Borrowed from Middle Dutch joncker (Dutch jonker, jonkheer), a compound equivalent to jong (“young”) + here (“lord”). Compare junker.

d.g: The quality or state of being young.
d.x: Her youth and beauty attracted him to her.

d.g: The part of life following childhood; the period of existence preceding maturity or age; the whole early part of life, from childhood, or, sometimes, from infancy, to adulthood.
d.x: Make the most of your youth, it will not last forever.

d.g: A young person.
d.x: There was a group of youths hanging around the parking lot, reading fashion magazines and listening to music.

d.g: A young man; a male adolescent or young adult.

youth.e: From Middle English youthe, youghte, ȝouþe, from Old English ġeoguþ (“the state of being young; youth”), from Proto-West Germanic *juwunþa, from Proto-Germanic *jugunþō, *jugunþiz (“youth”), corresponding to young + -th (abstract nominal suffix). …

d.g: The vitality characteristic of youth.

youthfulness.e: English youthful Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English youthfulness From youthful + -ness.

d.g: A prolonged, loud cry, like the sound of an animal; a wail; a howl.
Utter a yowl.
Express by yowling; utter with a yowl.

yowl.e: From Middle English youlen, goulen, from Old Norse gaula (“to low, bellow, howl, scream”), related to Icelandic gaula (“to yell, howl, roar”), Faroese geyla (“to bawl, squall, shout, yell, bellow”), Norwegian gaule (“to roar, howl, whine, weep noisily”), dialectal Swedish gjöla, Scots gowl (“to howl, yell, roar”), Shet …
